primary_meaning: The dragon symbolizes Satan (the devil) — the archenemy of God and his people, the ancient serpent who deceives, accuses, and persecutes, especially as portrayed in the book of Revelation.
primary_basis: Revelation 12:3-9 (the great red dragon, explicitly identified as 'that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan')
Revelation 12:13-17 (the dragon persecutes the woman and her offspring)
Revelation 13:2-4 (the dragon gives power and authority to the beast)
Revelation 16:13 (unclean spirits from the mouth of the dragon)
Revelation 20:2 (the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, bound for a thousand years)
Genesis 3:1-15 (the serpent in Eden, linked to the dragon via Revelation's 'ancient serpent' language)
Isaiah 27:1 (Leviathan the twisting serpent, the dragon in the sea, whom the LORD will slay)

alternatives.meaning: Chaos-monster / cosmic chaos motif: in Old Testament scholarship, dragon imagery (Leviathan, Rahab, tannin) draws on ancient Near Eastern combat myths and symbolizes primeval chaos that God subdues at creation and in salvation history.
Hostile pagan empires or rulers who oppress God's people, personified as dragons — notably Egypt/Pharaoh and Babylon; some interpreters extend this to Rome behind Revelation's dragon-beast imagery.
basis: Ezekiel 29:3 (Pharaoh as the great dragon in the Nile)
Isaiah 30:7 (Rahab as a name for Egypt)
Revelation 12-13 read against Roman imperial persecution

alternatives.meaning: In historicist Protestant interpretation, the dragon of Revelation 12 represents pagan Rome (and Satan working through it), which persecuted the early church and sought to destroy Christ.
basis: Revelation 12:1-5 read as the church/Israel bringing forth Christ under Roman rule

alternatives.meaning: A purely literary/mythological figure without theological referent — the dragon as a stock ancient monster image with no fixed symbolic meaning; largely a position in some critical scholarship rather than church teaching.
basis: Comparative studies of Ugaritic and Babylonian combat myths (Baal-Yam, Marduk-Tiamat) as background to biblical dragon language

notes: The identification of the dragon with Satan is unusually settled because Revelation 12:9 and 20:2 make the identification explicit within the text itself; virtually all Christian traditions (Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, evangelical, and most critical commentators on Revelation) accept it. The alternative readings are not so much rivals as complementary layers: OT dragon/sea-monster imagery (chaos, Leviathan, Rahab) and its application to oppressive empires (Egypt, Babylon, Rome) are widely seen as the background that Revelation gathers up into the figure of Satan. Disagreement among interpreters concerns the referents of the beasts and the timing of the dragon's defeat (preterist, historicist, futurist, idealist schemes), not the dragon's core identity as the devil.
